claims.text: Differences in mechanical properties among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its subsets are caused by variations in short-range order.
Differences in mechanical properties among these alloys are caused by variations in dislocation interactions.
Short-range order and dislocation interactions depend on the specific combination and concentration of constituent elements.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials after thermomechanical processing.
The intervention is systematic removal or variation of constituent elements to create quaternary and ternary subsets of the quinary alloy.
The controlled tests are room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests.
Short-range order and dislocation density are the proposed structural mediators.
Variations in short-range order affect dislocation mobility.
Variations in short-range order affect dislocation interactions.
Changes in dislocation mobility and interactions produce differences in work hardening and failure mechanisms.
The quinary alloy will have higher strength than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will have higher ductility than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The predicted strength and ductility advantages arise from greater complexity in short-range order and dislocation interactions in the quinary alloy.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase FCC microstructures tested at room temperature.
Finding no significant mechanical-property differences, or finding that the quinary alloy lacks the predicted strength and ductility advantage, would falsify the hypothesis.
